paragraphs: This paper asks whether deep classifiers can have something analogous to support vectors: examples that help reveal a model’s decision criteria. The motivation is to address two weaknesses of deep learning highlighted by the authors: demanding large training datasets and making decisions that are difficult to interpret. They introduce DeepKKT, an adaptation of the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker condition to deep learning.

Using this condition, the authors generate Deep Support Vectors and show that they share properties with traditional support vectors. These generated examples support few-shot dataset distillation, where a small collection of examples serves as a compact training resource. They also provide a way to examine classification behavior, helping reduce the model’s opacity.

The paper additionally uses DeepKKT to turn conventional classifiers into generators, with class labels serving as latent variables. The authors report high-fidelity generation and evaluate their approach on ImageNet, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 using ResNet and ConvNet architectures. Together, these results connect compact training data, interpretability, and generation through one condition on a classifier.
neurips-2024-deep-support-vectors-7bd748.tldr: DeepKKT identifies support-vector-like examples in deep classifiers, enabling compact dataset distillation, greater interpretability, and image generation.

paragraphs: When an optimization objective depends on a parameter, it can be useful to know how its solution changes as that parameter changes. Hyperparameter optimization is one example. This paper studies whether differentiating the successive updates of stochastic gradient descent, or SGD, yields an accurate estimate of that sensitivity.

The authors show that these derivatives follow another optimization process: an inexact SGD recursion on a different objective. The original SGD process introduces a perturbation into this second process as it approaches its solution. This connection makes it possible to analyze derivative accuracy through the behavior of a related stochastic optimization problem.

For strongly convex objectives, the authors establish mean-squared-error results for approaching the derivative of the solution mapping. With constant step sizes, derivative estimates settle within a noise region around the target. With shrinking step sizes, the stated convergence rate is O(log(k)^2/k). They additionally prove exponential convergence in the interpolation regime. Numerical experiments on synthetic tasks illustrate these theoretical findings, whose conclusions depend on the specified optimization setting.
neurips-2024-derivatives-of-stochastic-g.tldr: Under strong convexity, derivatives through SGD approach solution sensitivities with behavior determined by the step-size schedule and optimization regime.

paragraphs: Emotion analysis often examines people from an outside observer’s viewpoint. This paper instead develops resources for understanding emotion in first-person video, a perspective relevant to agents that experience and interact with their surroundings. Its central contribution is E³, a dataset containing more than 50 hours of everyday recordings spanning eight emotion types, different scenarios, and multiple languages.

The recordings provide visual, acoustic, and textual information about emotions in real situations. More than 80,000 manually created annotations support four benchmark tasks: emotion recognition, classification, localization, and reasoning. These tasks make the dataset useful for evaluating several aspects of emotion understanding rather than treating the problem as a single prediction exercise.

The authors also introduce Emotion-LlaMa, which combines acoustic information with visual input to improve understanding of first-person videos. Their comparison experiments report stronger performance than the evaluated baselines. The dataset and model establish a foundation for studying embodied emotion; applications to robotics, augmented reality, and more empathetic agents are presented as potential future benefits.
neurips-2024-e-3-exploring-embodied-emot.tldr: E³ supplies annotated first-person videos for emotion research, alongside a model that combines visual and acoustic cues.

paragraphs: Three-dimensional medical image segmentation requires models to identify structures throughout a volume. Although deep networks perform well at this task, their size and computational demands can make deployment difficult on hardware with limited resources. E2ENet addresses this problem through two architectural choices intended to preserve useful spatial information while reducing the expense of processing it.

The first is dynamic sparse feature fusion. It learns which information from different scales is useful to combine, reducing redundant feature processing. The second is restricted depth-shift in three-dimensional convolution. This design uses spatial information across the volume while keeping parameter and computational complexity at the level of methods based on two-dimensional processing.

The authors evaluate E2ENet on AMOS, Brain Tumor Segmentation, and the BTCV Challenge. Across the resource constraints studied, they report a better balance between segmentation accuracy and efficiency than previous approaches. The contribution is therefore a combination of selective feature fusion and economical spatial processing, aimed at making accurate volumetric segmentation more practical under limited computing budgets.
neurips-2024-e2enet-dynamic-sparse-featu.tldr: E2ENet combines selective feature fusion with economical 3D spatial processing to improve the accuracy–efficiency balance in medical image segmentation.

paragraphs: The effect of a treatment can vary across people or groups. Estimating these differences from observational data is difficult when unobserved factors influence both treatment and outcome. Instrumental variables, such as randomized recommendations, offer another source of evidence, but they can be weak when people rarely respond to the assigned encouragement.

This paper combines observational and instrumental-variable data in a two-stage framework. It first learns conditional average treatment effects from observational data, accepting that these estimates may be biased. It then uses instrumental-variable evidence to make a correction weighted by compliance, taking advantage of differences in instrument strength across observed characteristics.

The proposed approach addresses settings with unobserved confounding and low compliance, including some subgroups with no compliance at all. The authors characterize convergence rates and evaluate the method in simulations. They also apply it to differences in the effects of 401(k) participation on wealth. The central idea is to combine broad observational information with corrective evidence whose strength varies across groups.
neurips-2024-estimating-heterogeneous-tr.tldr: A two-stage estimator corrects biased observational treatment-effect estimates using instrumental-variable evidence weighted by compliance.

paragraphs: A language model with strong text understanding does not automatically make a good prompt encoder for image generation. The authors observe that directly substituting a decoder-only language model into this role substantially worsens prompt following. They identify a mismatch between next-token prediction training and the discriminative text features needed by diffusion models, together with positional bias from the decoder architecture.

Their framework changes how language models are used for prompt encoding, strengthening the text representations and addressing the positional bias. It also supports combining multiple language models. Building on this framework, the authors introduce LI-DIT, a diffusion transformer designed to incorporate these language-model representations into text-to-image generation.

Experiments examine LI-DIT across different model and dataset sizes. The authors report stronger prompt understanding than the open-source and commercial systems they compare against, including Stable Diffusion 3, DALL-E 3, and Midjourney V6. The result emphasizes that transferring language understanding into image generation requires a suitable interface between the language model and the diffusion model.
neurips-2024-exploring-the-role-of-large.tldr: LI-DIT adapts decoder-only language models for diffusion prompt encoding, addressing training mismatch and positional bias to improve prompt understanding.

paragraphs: Federated learning brings together training contributions from clients whose data can differ substantially. Those differences complicate both learning a useful shared model and producing models that work well locally. FedGMKD addresses this problem with a prototype-based personalized learning framework that combines knowledge distillation with an aggregation rule sensitive to differences among clients.

Its Cluster Knowledge Fusion component uses Gaussian mixture models on each client to generate prototype features and soft predictions. These summaries support knowledge distillation while preserving data privacy. A second component, discrepancy-aware aggregation, weights client contributions according to both data quality and quantity, aiming to improve generalization across the clients’ different distributions.

The framework operates without public datasets or generative models on the server. The authors provide a theoretical convergence analysis and evaluate FedGMKD on benchmarks including SVHN, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100. They report improvements over state-of-the-art methods in both local and global accuracy under non-IID data. These findings support combining client-side knowledge summaries with aggregation that accounts for heterogeneous contributions.
neurips-2024-fedgmkd-an-efficient-protot.tldr: FedGMKD combines client-side prototype distillation with quality- and quantity-aware aggregation to improve federated learning on heterogeneous data.

paragraphs: Pretrained image diffusion models provide useful visual knowledge for generating 3D content, but their spatial mistakes can produce objects that disagree across viewpoints. In generation through Score Distillation Sampling, overfitting to particular views creates the inconsistency known as the Janus Problem. Hallo3D investigates these hallucinations and uses multimodal models to help identify them.

The authors find that large multimodal models can infer geometric structures even without geometric constraints. Their method represents queries about multimodal inconsistencies, detects specific hallucinations, and incorporates that information into an enhanced prompt. This guidance helps bring rendered views into agreement while jointly optimizing the 3D content’s structure and appearance across viewpoints.

Hallo3D requires neither tuning nor 3D training data and can be inserted into existing generation frameworks. The authors report substantial improvements in consistency and state-of-the-art performance relative to the optimization methods evaluated. The approach makes inferred geometric information useful as corrective guidance for generation, specifically targeting errors introduced by the pretrained models supplying the visual knowledge.
neurips-2024-hallo3d-multi-modal-halluci.tldr: Hallo3D uses multimodal hallucination detection to guide more consistent 3D generation without tuning or 3D training data.

paragraphs: This paper proposes Implicit Regularization Enhancement, or IRE, to help neural network training reach flat solutions more quickly. The approach distinguishes directions in parameter space where the training objective changes gently from directions where it changes sharply. Its purpose is to improve generalization and convergence by treating these different training dynamics separately.

IRE accelerates sharpness reduction along flat directions while maintaining stability along sharp ones. The authors describe it as a framework that can be incorporated into generic base optimizers without substantial computational overhead. This makes the contribution an enhancement to optimization procedures rather than a method tied to a single network architecture.

Image classification experiments report consistent generalization improvements across CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet, ResNets, and vision transformers. In pretraining Llama models ranging from 60 million to 229 million parameters, the authors report a twofold speedup over AdamW on the studied datasets. They also provide theoretical guarantees of faster convergence toward flat minima for Sharpness-aware Minimization. That theoretical result has a specific optimizer setting, alongside the broader empirical evidence.
neurips-2024-improving-generalization-an.tldr: IRE separates flat and sharp optimization dynamics, improving generalization and accelerating training in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Training tasks together and pretraining before fine-tuning can both encourage networks to reuse features, but they need not encourage the same kind of reuse. This paper characterizes those preferences through implicit regularization penalties in diagonal linear networks and single-hidden-layer ReLU networks. The analysis identifies a tradeoff between sharing features across tasks and keeping the learned feature set sparse.

A central finding is a nested feature selection regime in pretraining followed by fine-tuning. Here, the downstream task relies on a sparse subset of features learned during pretraining. This regime is much narrower in multi-task learning. The ReLU analysis also finds that sequential training benefits from features correlated across the auxiliary and main tasks, unlike multi-task learning in the studied setting.

The authors support these findings with teacher-student experiments and introduce weight rescaling after pretraining to encourage nested selection. In deep image classifiers, rescaling improves performance when it produces signatures of that regime. The results suggest that selective reuse of pretrained features may help explain fine-tuning’s effectiveness.
neurips-2024-inductive-biases-of-multi-t.tldr: The paper identifies how joint training and fine-tuning favor different feature reuse patterns, including sparse selection of pretrained features.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning an aligned chat model for a useful downstream task can increase unsafe behavior, even when the training data appears benign. This paper studies how to reduce that loss of alignment in the practical setting where a public model is customized before being served to users. It focuses on the prompt templates used during customization and deployment.

The authors propose Pure Tuning, Safe Testing, or PTST. The strategy omits a safety prompt during fine-tuning and adds one when the model is used at test time. This deliberately creates a difference between training and inference inputs, with the aim of encouraging the customized model to preserve its safety alignment.

Experiments involve Llama 2-Chat, Mistral 7B Instruct v0.2, and GPT-3.5 Turbo, with fine-tuning tasks drawn from GSM8K, ChatDoctor, and OpenOrca. The authors report that PTST substantially reduces the increase in unsafe behavior. The finding makes prompt-template choices an important part of managing alignment after customization, while the reported benefit concerns reduced deterioration rather than guaranteed safety.
neurips-2024-keeping-llms-aligned-after-.tldr: Omitting safety prompts during fine-tuning and adding them at inference reduces alignment loss in the reported chat-model experiments.

paragraphs: Understanding how a language model expresses a fact requires examining how its internal components work together. This paper studies knowledge circuits in the model’s computation graph, extending the focus beyond isolated attention heads or multilayer perceptrons. The aim is to identify connected computations involved in articulating particular pieces of knowledge.

Experiments with GPT2 and TinyLLAMA reveal collaboration among information heads, relation heads, and multilayer perceptrons. This circuit perspective links the roles of individual components to the larger computation that produces a knowledge-bearing response. The authors also examine how existing knowledge editing techniques affect these circuits, using those effects to investigate how the techniques work and where their constraints arise.

The paper further uses knowledge circuits to interpret hallucinations and in-context learning. These analyses make circuits a tool for studying both stored knowledge and observable model behavior. The authors present better understanding of Transformers and improved knowledge editing as promising directions supported by this perspective, rather than claiming that circuit analysis already resolves those broader challenges.
neurips-2024-knowledge-circuits-in-pretr.tldr: Knowledge circuits reveal how interacting Transformer components express facts and provide a lens on editing, hallucinations, and in-context learning.

paragraphs: Removing selected knowledge from a language model is difficult because information to forget can overlap with information to retain. Updating a large model can also be computationally expensive. ECO addresses these problems by enforcing forgetting behavior during inference, using modified prompt embeddings rather than relying on the language model itself to unlearn.

A prompt classifier identifies requests associated with knowledge designated for forgetting. Offline, zeroth-order optimization learns corruptions to add to prompt embeddings. During inference, those corruptions are applied to prompts flagged by the classifier. This separates the decision about which requests need intervention from the learned modification that changes the model’s response.

The authors report outputs that satisfy the unlearning objective and closely resemble those of a model never trained on the designated data. Their experiments find nearly zero side effects in general and closely related domains. They also demonstrate the method across 100 models ranging from 0.5 billion to 236 billion parameters, reporting no additional method cost as parameter count increases. These are results about controlled inference behavior, not removal of information from model weights.
neurips-2024-large-language-model-unlear.tldr: ECO induces unlearning-like behavior by detecting targeted prompts and modifying their embeddings at inference time.

paragraphs: Mamba models process long sequences with computation that grows linearly with sequence length, making them attractive for applications such as language modeling. This paper addresses a complementary need: explaining their predictions. It adapts Layer-wise Relevance Propagation, or LRP, to trace a model’s output back through its internal computations.

The authors use relevance conservation as a guiding principle, tracking how explanatory relevance is distributed through the network. They identify particular Mamba components that produce unfaithful explanations under relevance propagation. MambaLRP modifies the propagation procedure for these components to make the resulting explanations more stable and reliable.

The authors report theoretical support and state-of-the-art explanation performance across the models and datasets evaluated. They also use MambaLRP to inspect architectural biases and assess their significance. Another application examines earlier speculation about Mamba’s long-range capabilities. The contribution therefore includes both an explanation algorithm and a means of investigating model behavior, without the abstract claiming a particular resolution to every question about long-range processing.
neurips-2024-mambalrp-explaining-selecti.tldr: MambaLRP adapts relevance propagation to Mamba’s architecture, improving explanations and enabling closer study of biases and long-range behavior.

paragraphs: Communication helps cooperating agents deal with incomplete observations and unpredictable environments. Yet sharing information does not fully solve coordination: an agent’s action may depend on what others choose, while their choices depend on its own. SeqComm addresses this circular dependency by giving agents an order in which to make and communicate decisions.

The method has two communication phases. During negotiation, agents exchange hidden representations of their observations and compare the value of their intentions, estimated using a model of environment dynamics. This establishes decision-making priority. During launching, higher-priority agents choose actions first and communicate those actions to lower-priority agents, which then make their own decisions.

This sequence gives later decision makers access to actual earlier choices, rather than requiring everyone to settle mutually dependent actions simultaneously. The authors provide a theoretical result that policies learned by SeqComm improve monotonically and converge. Experiments on a variety of cooperative multi-agent tasks also show better performance than the existing methods evaluated, supporting ordered communication as a coordination mechanism.
neurips-2024-multi-agent-coordination-vi.tldr: SeqComm coordinates agents by negotiating decision priorities and then sharing actions sequentially.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction expresses uncertainty through a set of possible labels designed to include the correct label at a specified coverage level. Adaptive methods extend this idea to changing data distributions. This paper addresses a further difficulty: the model that produces efficient prediction sets at one time may become a poor choice after the environment changes.

The proposed framework chooses among multiple candidate models as new data arrives. Instead of committing permanently to one model, it selects the model used to construct prediction sets on the fly. This adds adaptation at the model-selection level, allowing the prediction procedure to respond when unknown distribution shifts change which candidate works best.

The authors prove strongly adaptive regret over all intervals while maintaining valid coverage. This provides a theoretical performance statement across time intervals alongside the coverage result. Experiments on real and synthetic datasets report more efficient prediction sets than alternative methods while preserving valid coverage. The stated benefit is improved usefulness of the uncertainty sets without giving up their coverage objective.
neurips-2024-multi-model-ensemble-confor.tldr: Selecting conformal prediction models on the fly improves prediction-set efficiency under distribution shifts while maintaining valid coverage.

paragraphs: Prompt tuning can improve recognition in large models that analyze 3D point clouds while updating relatively few parameters. This paper observes a substantial tradeoff: better performance on a downstream task can accompany much worse generalization across 3D domains. Point-PRC aims to preserve the model’s broader knowledge while it learns task-specific prompts.

The framework places several explicit constraints on the prompt-learning process. These encourage agreement between predictions tailored to the task and the general knowledge already learned by the large 3D model. By making the prompts interact with that knowledge, the method regulates how specialization develops. It is designed as a module that can be added to existing representative models.

The authors report improvements in both domain generalization and task-specific recognition across the benchmarks studied. They also introduce three evaluation settings: base-to-new, cross-dataset, and few-shot generalization. Together, the method and benchmarks address how to assess and improve adaptation beyond the immediate training task, with the reported results showing that stronger specialization and broader generalization can coexist.
neurips-2024-point-prc-a-prompt-learning.tldr: Point-PRC constrains prompt tuning to retain general 3D knowledge, improving both recognition and domain generalization in the reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: Image reconstruction from indirect measurements can have multiple plausible answers. Bayesian inverse methods describe this uncertainty through a posterior distribution, combining measurement evidence with prior knowledge about images. Diffusion models provide expressive image priors, but the authors identify a problem with many existing approaches: approximations used for flexibility can distort the distribution of reconstructed samples.

The paper proposes a Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm that reduces posterior sampling for general inverse problems to posterior sampling for Gaussian denoising. A general formulation of diffusion models provides a common interface for rigorously solving that denoising problem. This allows the method to use a range of diffusion models while avoiding the generative approximations targeted by the paper.

Evaluation covers six inverse problems, split between three linear and three nonlinear cases, including real-world black hole imaging. The authors report more accurate reconstructions and posterior estimates than the diffusion-based imaging methods compared. The contribution concerns both producing convincing reconstructed images and better representing the range of possibilities supported by the Bayesian formulation.
neurips-2024-principled-probabilistic-im.tldr: A Monte Carlo method uses diffusion models through Gaussian denoising to improve Bayesian image reconstruction and posterior estimation.

paragraphs: A mixture-of-experts model uses a gating function to control how expert predictions contribute to its output. Softmax is a common choice, but its structure can encourage competition among experts and potentially contribute to representation collapse. This paper provides a theoretical comparison with sigmoid gating, focusing specifically on how efficiently the individual expert functions can be estimated from data.

The analysis considers regression with least-squares estimation when the fitted model contains more experts than the true regression function. Within this over-specified setting, the authors identify two gating regimes. For each, they formulate an identifiability condition for the expert functions and derive convergence rates, making the conditions for the comparison part of the result.

For feed-forward experts using common activations such as ReLU and GELU, the derived rates favor sigmoid gating over softmax in both regimes. With the same expert choice, sigmoid gating needs fewer samples to attain a given expert-estimation error. This establishes a sample-efficiency advantage in the analyzed statistical setting, rather than a universal claim about every mixture-of-experts application.
neurips-2024-sigmoid-gating-is-more-samp.tldr: Under the analyzed regression and identifiability conditions, sigmoid gating estimates experts more sample-efficiently than softmax gating.

paragraphs: Low-rank weight representations can reduce the parameters and memory needed to train language models, but they restrict weights to a low-dimensional space. The authors argue that this restriction is generally more problematic for pretraining from scratch than for fine-tuning. SLTrain addresses it by representing each weight matrix as the sum of a low-rank matrix and a sparse matrix.

The low-rank part is learned through matrix factorization. For the sparse part, the method randomly selects a fixed set of positions and learns only their values. Those positions do not need to change during training. This simple addition gives the representation flexibility beyond the low-rank component while introducing relatively few extra trainable entries.

The authors report substantially better pretraining performance than low-rank parameterization alone, with minimal additional parameter and memory costs and performance comparable to full-rank training. Combined with quantization and per-layer updates, SLTrain reduces memory requirements by up to 73% when pretraining LLaMA 7B. That memory result applies to the combined configuration described in the paper.
neurips-2024-sltrain-a-sparse-plus-low-r.tldr: SLTrain combines low-rank weights with a fixed sparse component to make language-model pretraining more parameter- and memory-efficient.

paragraphs: Answering questions about a scientific paper often requires understanding its figures and tables alongside its prose. SPIQA targets this kind of reading, addressing the limited scale and text-only focus of existing scientific question-answering datasets. It covers computer science research articles and asks models to interpret visual material in the context of the surrounding paper.

The dataset is built through automatic and manual curation using multimodal language models. Its information-seeking task includes interleaved text and multiple images, spanning plots, charts, tables, schematic diagrams, and visualized results. SPIQA contains 270,000 questions organized into training, validation, and three evaluation splits, providing a substantial resource for studying these combined reading demands.

The authors evaluate 12 foundational models and propose a chain-of-thought evaluation strategy with in-context retrieval. They report that this strategy supports detailed step-by-step assessment and improves performance. They also examine how much additional textual information can help. These contributions make SPIQA both a benchmark for current multimodal systems and a resource for exploring better access to scientific information.
neurips-2024-spiqa-a-dataset-for-multimo.tldr: SPIQA provides 270,000 questions for evaluating how models combine figures, tables, and text to understand scientific papers.

paragraphs: Producing several text-completion drafts ordinarily requires repeatedly running a language model. Superposed Decoding aims to generate k drafts at the computational cost of one autoregressive inference pass. Its key idea is to combine the latest token embeddings from the different drafts into a superposition that becomes the input to the next decoding step.

At each step, the algorithm combines the k current drafts with the top k tokens, forming k squared candidate continuations. It then retains the k most likely candidates. An n-gram interpolation procedure helps filter incoherent generations with little computational overhead. This maintains several draft candidates while sharing the expensive language-model computation across them.

In the reported experiments, the drafts are at least as coherent as nucleus sampling outputs and as factual as greedy decoding outputs, with at least a 2.44-fold speedup for k of three or more. Users also prefer its outputs over nucleus sampling under matched compute. The authors report further coverage gains when combining the method with other decoding strategies as inference compute increases.
neurips-2024-superposed-decoding-multipl.tldr: Superposed Decoding shares a language-model inference pass across multiple drafts, reducing computation while preserving quality in the reported comparisons.

paragraphs: Human image animation takes a reference picture of a person and a target motion video, then generates that person performing the motion. The authors identify a source of inconsistent quality in diffusion-based systems: the person’s scale and rotation in the reference image may differ from those in the target pose. Such mismatches can reduce fidelity and consistency.

Test-time Procrustes Calibration, or TPC, addresses this issue by supplying a calibrated reference image to the diffusion model. The adjustment helps the model establish correspondence between the human shapes in the reference and target images. It targets the input composition that affects animation quality, allowing the existing generator to work with a better-aligned reference.

The authors present TPC as a simple, model-agnostic method applicable to diffusion-based image animation systems without additional training. They report improved robustness when reference and target compositions are misaligned, a situation described as common in real-world use. The practical contribution is an inference-time calibration step intended to preserve animation quality across differences in scale and rotation.
neurips-2024-tpc-test-time-procrustes-ca.tldr: TPC calibrates reference images at inference time to improve diffusion-based human animation when body scale and rotation differ.

paragraphs: A single prediction does not describe the range of outcomes that might occur. Probabilistic prediction instead estimates a distribution, supporting uncertainty assessment, risk calculations, and outlier detection. Treeffuser addresses tabular regression problems where standard assumptions about the shape of that distribution, such as a Gaussian or Poisson form, may fit poorly.

The method learns a conditional diffusion model whose score function is estimated by gradient-boosted trees. The diffusion component supplies flexibility without requiring a fixed parametric response distribution. The tree component makes the method robust and straightforward to train on CPUs. Together, they support responses with several variables, multiple peaks, or asymmetric distributions.

On synthetic and real datasets, the authors report better-calibrated probabilistic predictions and stronger performance than the existing methods evaluated. They also demonstrate an inventory-allocation application using Walmart sales data. This connects distribution modeling to a decision problem where uncertainty matters: the value of the prediction comes from representing possible outcomes, rather than supplying only a central estimate.
neurips-2024-treeffuser-probabilistic-pr.tldr: Treeffuser combines conditional diffusion with gradient-boosted trees to produce flexible, well-calibrated predictive distributions for tabular data.

paragraphs: A vision-language model can give conflicting answers about the same visual fact when the prompt changes the range of possible answers. This paper introduces ConBench to examine that inconsistency systematically. The benchmark varies a prompt’s solution space around a common knowledge point, testing whether different ways of asking remain compatible.

The authors report that discriminative question accuracy falls as the solution space grows. They also find a strong positive correlation between discriminative accuracy and agreement with the model’s caption. This connects answers that distinguish among possibilities with freely generated descriptions. In the evaluated comparisons, closed-source models show a pronounced consistency advantage that the authors characterize in terms of bias.

The paper then applies trigger-based diagnostic refinement to improve consistency, reporting an indirect improvement in caption performance as well. These findings make agreement across prompt forms an additional dimension of model evaluation. A model’s ability to answer one question correctly does not, by itself, describe how consistently it expresses the same visual knowledge across different questions and captions.
neurips-2024-unveiling-the-tapestry-of-c.tldr: ConBench reveals inconsistencies across vision-language prompt formats, and diagnostic refinement improves agreement and caption performance.
